summary: Defines a URI- and header-friendly envelope for carrying symmetrically encrypted, authenticated and timestamped tokens, and describes one usage as a simple cookie-based protocol. This is KoanLogic's Secure Cookie Sessions. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A sealed note you hand to a browser to carry. Only the website can open it, and the note shows nobody changed it.

questions: what is the scs cookie format
subtitle: Encrypting and signing HTTP cookies so the browser carries secure state.

tldr.problem: Web servers often need to store session state on the server side, which requires shared storage or database lookups. For embedded devices, routers, or load-balanced services, keeping state on the client side is simpler but requires the cookie to be tamper-proof and confidential.
tldr.mechanism: SCS wraps session data in a cookie with encryption (AES-CBC-128), authentication (HMAC-SHA1), and a timestamp. The server encrypts the state and signs it; the client stores the opaque cookie and returns it on the next request. The server decrypts and verifies it.
tldr.outcome: The server avoids storing session state, making it suitable for stateless architectures, embedded systems, and high-availability deployments. The trade-off is that security relies entirely on the encryption keys and the application must handle replay, deletion, and fixation risks that the protocol does not.

today: RFC 6896 is an Informational RFC published in March 2013 and has not been obsoleted. It remains the specification for SCS and is suitable for embedded systems, routers, and stateless services that need encrypted session cookies.

sections.title: What SCS Does
sections.content:
Secure Cookie Sessions (SCS) is a way to let HTTP servers put encrypted and signed information in a cookie. Instead of storing session state on the server, the server encrypts the state, signs it with an authentication tag, and sends it to the client in a cookie. The client stores the cookie and returns it with each request, the same way it returns any cookie.

SCS is designed for servers that have no reliable storage, cannot easily share state in a cluster, or want to move session management to the client. It is also URI-friendly, meaning SCS tokens can be embedded in URLs or used in authorization tokens.
sections.eli5: Instead of the server remembering who you are in a database, the server puts that information in an encrypted envelope, gives it to you, and asks you to give it back next time. The encryption means you cannot peek inside or change it.

sections.title: The Cookie Structure
sections.content:
An SCS cookie holds five pieces of information, each base64url-encoded and separated by a pipe character (|).

DATA is the encrypted session state. ATIME is a Unix timestamp of when the server last saw this cookie; the server uses it to expire old sessions. TID is a transform identifier that tells the server which encryption and signing keys to use. IV is a random initialization vector used for encryption, making each cookie unique even if the state is the same. AUTHTAG is an HMAC signature that proves the cookie has not been altered.

The cookie value looks like: eDATA|eATIME|eTID|eIV|eAUTHTAG. Only the DATA field is encrypted; the others are base64-encoded plaintext. The signature covers all five fields, so changing any of them breaks the authentication.
sections.eli5: The cookie is like an envelope with five labeled parts: your encrypted data, when you last visited, which key was used, a random number for extra security, and a signature seal. If you change any part, the seal breaks and the server knows.

sections.title: Encryption and Signing
sections.content:
SCS uses AES-128 in CBC mode to encrypt the session data. Before encryption, the data is optionally compressed with DEFLATE to save space. Each encryption gets a fresh random initialization vector (IV) to prevent an attacker from spotting patterns across multiple cookies.

Authentication is handled with HMAC-SHA1. The server computes an HMAC over the pipe-separated string of base64-encoded fields. The pipes are important: they serve as explicit length markers, preventing an attacker from rearranging or merging fields.

The RFC mandates that encryption and authentication use separate keys. Implementers SHOULD consider using 256-bit keys for higher security, though 128-bit keys are the minimum. If a server needs to rotate keys (changing the TID), it must keep the old key available for a transition period so active sessions do not break.
sections.eli5: The server scrambles your data with a key, adds a checksum seal, and gives you the locked envelope. Even if someone steals it, they cannot open it or change it without the key and they would break the seal.

sections.title: How Cookies Are Used
sections.content:
The server creates an SCS cookie by encrypting the plaintext session data with AES, recording the current time in ATIME, looking up the keys by TID, generating a random IV, and computing the AUTHTAG. It sends this as a Set-Cookie header with standard cookie attributes like Expires, Domain, Secure, and HttpOnly.

The client stores the cookie and sends it back in future requests, just like any HTTP cookie. When the server receives it, it splits the five fields, looks up the keys using TID, verifies the AUTHTAG, checks that ATIME has not exceeded the session timeout, and decrypts and decompresses the DATA. If any step fails—wrong signature, expired timestamp, or unknown TID—the cookie is rejected.
sections.eli5: Server seals a note and hands it to you. You bring it back on your next visit. Server opens the note, checks nobody tampered with it, checks it is not too old, and reads what is inside.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
SCS protects the cookie from tampering and eavesdropping, but it does not prevent all session attacks. An attacker who steals an old cookie can replay it (use it again later) until the timestamp expires. The application must add its own protection if replay resistance is critical, such as by embedding a nonce in the data, binding the cookie to a TLS session, or using a list of invalidated cookies.

A malicious client can delete a cookie and send no cookie at all. The application must not rely on a cookie to enforce negative permissions (like banning a user); instead, use the cookie for positive capabilities.

SCS does not protect against session fixation (where an attacker tricks a client into using an attacker-controlled session ID) because the browser plays no active role. A more sophisticated protocol with challenge-response would be needed.

On the positive side, SCS avoids the server-side risks of session identifier prediction and brute-forcing. As long as the encryption key is secret, an attacker cannot forge, alter, or decrypt a cookie without knowing the key.
sections.eli5: The sealed note is safe from changes and prying eyes, but if someone steals it before you read it, they can use it. And you can throw away the note (the server cannot stop you). The server should design the note so throwing it away does not help an attacker.

sections.title: Use Cases and Size Trade-offs
sections.content:
SCS is useful for SOHO routers, embedded devices, and load-balanced web services that need session state but cannot easily share a database. The application is responsible for managing keys and rotations; the SCS envelope itself is stateless.

SCS cookies are larger than plaintext cookies. Base64 encoding expands data by about 1.33 times, and there is a fixed overhead of roughly 80 to 90 bytes for the encrypted state, timestamp, TID, IV, and signature. Small amounts of data (under 100 bytes plaintext) may double in size, but large session states absorb the overhead better.
sections.eli5: Stateless servers that do not keep a database can use SCS to let browsers carry their own session info safely. The trade-off is that cookies are a bit bulkier because of encryption and signing.
